sections.heading: Two search results, two different games

blocks.text: Type "plumber" into Google from your phone and you get two things: the map pack with three businesses, and the regular results underneath. They are ranked by different systems.

blocks.title: The map pack
blocks.text: Your Google Business Profile: its category, its reviews, its distance from the searcher.

blocks.title: The regular results
blocks.text: Your website: a page for that service in that city, and the links pointing at it.

Winning one does not win the other, which is why so many local SEO services post to your profile every week and never move anything. We work both, in the order that matters. Our guide to [ranking higher on Google Maps](/blog/how-to-rank-higher-on-google-maps-a-comprehensive-guide) explains the map side in full if you want the long version first.

sections.heading: What actually ranks a Google Business Profile

blocks.text: The factors are measured every year by [Whitespark's Local Search Ranking Factors](https://whitespark.ca/local-search-ranking-factors/) survey, and the 2026 edition is blunt. The primary category is factor one of 187. Reviews, their recency, and a steady flow of them are the fastest rising signals. Keywords in the services field jumped from factor 110 to 35 in a single year. Google posts sit at 148.

So that is our order. Primary category read off the top three competitors in your market, not guessed. Every predefined service Google offers for your category, plus custom ones under the names customers actually search. Then a review process that runs every week: a direct link sent after the job, no gating, no incentives, and a reply from you within 48 hours. Then hours, attributes, description, and 8 to 12 real photos, because Google's Ask Maps answers questions straight from those fields now that Q&A is gone. The field by field detail is in our [Google Business Profile guide](/blog/google-business-profile-optimization-guide-2026).

We do not geotag photos. Google strips the location data on upload and the published tests show no effect. We do not stuff the business name with keywords, because that is the top cause of suspensions. And we do not post for the sake of posting.

sections.heading: What ranks your website locally

blocks.text: A dedicated page for each service you sell, written for your city, is the number one local organic factor. Not a homepage that lists nine services, not a city page with the name swapped in. A real page, with your work, your reviews from that city, and an answer to the question at the top.

We build those pages, wire them into your profile, and link them from the pages on your site that already get traffic. If the site itself is too old or too slow to carry them, we rebuild it; see [website design for small businesses](/services/websites). The site wide work that sits under all of this is on our [SEO services](/services/seo) page.

sections.heading: Storefronts, service areas, and several towns

blocks.title: Storefront or service area
blocks.text: A storefront shows its address and ranks around it. A service area business, the plumber or landscaper who works from home, hides the address and lists the towns it serves, and it ranks strongest near home. Both are legitimate; pretending to be the other one is the second most common reason a profile gets suspended.

blocks.title: Several towns
blocks.text: If you serve several towns, we do not build a page for every town times every service. We start with the smaller towns nobody else is targeting, one page per town, each with something real about that place and your work there. A landscaper serving five towns gets five pages over five weeks, not fifty in a weekend, because Google reads a batch of near identical pages as a doorway scheme and buries the whole domain.

sections.heading: Citations, reviews, and AI answers

blocks.title: Citations, done once
blocks.text: Citations are your name, phone, and address on the directories that matter: Google, Apple, Bing, Facebook, Yelp, then the industry ones for your trade. We build 25 to 40 of them, by hand, from one canonical record, and then stop. Diminishing returns start there. We never rent citations on a monthly sync, because when the subscription ends, most of the listings decay with it.

blocks.title: Reviews without the risk
blocks.text: Reviews gate entry to the map pack, and nearly half of consumers will not use a business with fewer than 20. So the review ask has to become a habit, not a campaign. We set up the automation: one message after each job, a direct unfiltered link to your profile, a reply template for you, and nothing that pre screens the customer's mood first. Google rewrote its review policy in 2026, and the FTC fines for fake or gated reviews run to $53,088 per violation. Doing it properly is not optional anymore.

blocks.title: When they ask an AI instead
blocks.text: More people ask ChatGPT or Google's AI for "a good electrician near me" than a year ago. Those answers are built from the pages that already rank and from the directories and lists the models read, so most of the work above counts twice. The rest is format: an answer at the top of each page in plain text, and real mentions on the review sites. We wrote up the specifics in [AEO for local businesses](/blog/aeo-for-local-businesses).

sections.heading: How you will see progress

blocks.text: Every week we scan a 49 point grid across your service area and show you where you rank at each point, in green and red, next to your competitors. It is the same scan we run on our own [Bakersfield profile](/bakersfield/seo), which started at zero on every point. You see proximity for what it is: you will rank strongest near your address and fade with distance, and no tactic changes that. Website pages and links are what reach past it.
Month one we report the profile completeness, review count, and the first grid. Month three, the grid moving on your easiest terms. Month six, calls and direction requests from the profile.

Your list of customers from the last three months, so the first review asks go to people who remember you. And one exact spelling of your business name, phone, and address, which every listing will then copy.

faqs.a: It depends on how far you are from the pack today. A business with a verified profile, a decent site, and a handful of reviews needs a one off setup plus a light monthly retainer for the review process and the grid tracking. A business starting from nothing needs the profile built, a page per service, and citations first. faqs.q: I work from home. Can I still rank without showing my address?

faqs.q: Do Google posts help me rank?
faqs.a: Barely. Posting frequency is factor 148 of 187 and posting quantity is 168. Posts are useful as fresh material for Ask Maps and as a place to put a call to action, so we schedule one a week, but if the posts are the whole plan, the plan is wrong.

sections.heading: What programmatic SEO is

blocks.text: A template, a dataset, and a rule that turns each row into a page. A lender publishes a page per city with real rate data. A software company publishes a page per integration. A directory publishes a page per product and location.

The pages rank because each one answers a search nobody has bothered to answer on its own, and there are hundreds of those searches. That is the promise, and it is real. Zillow, TripAdvisor, and NerdWallet are programmatic sites at heart.

sections.heading: When it works, and when it is spam

blocks.title: Google's own definition
blocks.text: Google's [spam policies](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies) name the failure mode directly. Scaled content abuse is "many pages generated for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users." Doorway abuse is pages "created to rank for specific, similar search queries" that lead to a weaker destination. A city page with the name swapped and nothing else changed is both.

blocks.title: Our test for every page
blocks.text: Does this page carry something no other page on the internet has? Your own numbers, your own inventory, your own measurements, a calculator, a comparison built from live data. If the answer is yes, the set can be large. If the answer is a paragraph of generic text and a different city in the H1, we will not build it, and we will say why on the call.

sections.heading: How we build a page set

blocks.title: Research first
blocks.text: We pull real search volume for the combinations you think people search, and we read the live results for a sample of them, because half the time the intent is not what the keyword tool says.

blocks.title: The data model
blocks.text: The page set is a product fed by a database, not a batch of articles, so we design the data model before the template. Where the data has to be pulled from somewhere, our [custom builds](/services/custom-builds) team writes the pipeline.

blocks.title: A small first batch
blocks.text: The first batch is a test, not a launch. We ran that test on ourselves. In March 2026 we published 12 industry pages on our own site, one per keyword cluster, linked from the industries grid on our [services page](/services), and gated the second batch on Google indexing the first. Five months later only 2 of the 12 had earned a single impression in Search Console. So the second batch never got built, and those pages are being rewritten one at a time with data each page can call its own. That is the gate working. "Crawled, currently not indexed" is Google telling you the pages are thin, and publishing more of them makes it worse.

blocks.title: Internal links, then the next batch
blocks.text: Links from the pages that already get traffic, because an orphaned page set dies quietly no matter how good the template is. Only then does the next batch go out.

sections.heading: What we refuse to build

blocks.text: A services times cities matrix. Pages for towns you do not serve. A template that ships with a city name and nothing local underneath it. Three hundred pages in a week on a domain that has never published thirty. Each of these has cost someone their rankings, and the June 2026 spam update was unusually fast about it.
If your customers are in one or two cities, you do not need programmatic SEO. You need a real page per service, and that is [local SEO](/services/seo/local).

sections.heading: Where it fits

blocks.text: Programmatic SEO services sit on top of the ordinary work: the money pages, the weekly content, the technical foundation covered on our [SEO services](/services/seo) page. They are a multiplier, not a substitute. The same domain that grew to 204 ranked keywords in 6 months carries our own industry pages, and you can see how the two fit together in the [organic growth case study](/work/rsla-organic-growth).

faqHeading: Questions people ask about programmatic SEO

faqs.q: What is programmatic SEO?
faqs.a: Publishing a set of pages from one template and one dataset, so that each search variation gets its own page without writing each one by hand. It works when every page contains data that is genuinely different and genuinely useful. It fails when the pages are the same text with one word swapped.

faqs.q: Is programmatic SEO against Google's guidelines?
faqs.a: The technique is not. Thin, near identical pages built to catch searches are, under Google's scaled content abuse and doorway policies, and the penalty is applied to the domain, not just the pages. The line is whether each page helps the person who lands on it.

faqs.q: How many pages should we start with?
faqs.a: Fewer than you think. A first batch small enough to watch, usually 10 to 20, published on a site that already has some authority, then the rest in batches as each one gets indexed. A brand new domain cannot absorb 200 pages at once and we will not pretend otherwise.

faqs.q: Does programmatic SEO work for a small business?
faqs.a: Only if the business has the data. A landscaper has a handful of services and a few towns, which is a local SEO job. A landscaper with pricing for 60 plant varieties by yard size has a page set. We check which one you are before quoting.

sections.heading: What SEO is in 2026

blocks.text: Search engine optimization used to mean pleasing an algorithm. It now means answering real customer questions with real expertise, one page at a time. Google's own guidance says the same thing in more words: publish [helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) written for people.

The AI assistants changed less than people think. ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google's AI Overviews build their answers from the pages that already rank. Rank on Google and the citations follow. So the ranking work is the AI work. We do not sell them as two separate things. If your customers are local, our guide to [showing up in ChatGPT as a local business](/blog/aeo-for-local-businesses) covers the specifics.

sections.heading: What our SEO services for small business owners include

blocks.title: Money pages first

If a page for the thing you sell does not exist, nothing else matters yet. Our [websites](/services/websites) are built with this structure from day one.

blocks.title: On page SEO

blocks.title: One article a week
blocks.text: Genuinely useful, built from questions your customers already ask, wired into the pages that make money. Consistency is what wins. Almost nobody keeps it up, which is exactly why it works.

blocks.title: Technical SEO underneath

sections.heading: How a keyword gets chosen

blocks.title: Search Console first

blocks.title: Real search volume

blocks.title: The live top ten, read by a person
blocks.text: The volume tools are wrong about intent more often than they are right. A term that looks commercial can turn out to be job listings and university guides when you look.
Only then does a keyword get a page. One keyword, one page, and never two pages chasing the same intent, because Google will rank neither.

sections.heading: Where the weekly article goes

blocks.text: Each article answers one question a real customer asked, in your words, from your experience. It links to the service page it supports, and three older articles get a link back to it, because that is how a new page gets noticed without waiting months. Over a year that is roughly fifty pages of answers, all pointing at the pages that sell. That is the snowball, and it is the whole method.

sections.heading: Local and programmatic

blocks.title: Local SEO
blocks.text: If your customers are in one city, the work shifts toward Google Maps, your Business Profile, reviews, and a page per service in that city. That is [local SEO](/services/seo/local), and it has its own page because it has its own rules. If you are in Kern County, we do it in person; see [SEO in Bakersfield](/bakersfield/seo).

blocks.title: Programmatic SEO

sections.heading: How we think about it

blocks.text: Never touch a page that already ranks in the top three. Match what ranks, never a fixed word count. One keyword per page, always. Fix the thin page before adding ten more. These rules are unglamorous, and they are the difference between a site that climbs and one that gets buried by the next core update.

A national online store with ten thousand products needs an ecommerce specialist. A company that wants a report every week instead of a page every week is going to be disappointed. sections.heading: Signs it is time to redesign

blocks.title: It fails on a phone
blocks.text: The site does not work on a phone, or it does, but you have to pinch and zoom.

blocks.title: It loads slowly
blocks.text: It takes four seconds to load on 5G, and most of your visitors are on a phone.

blocks.title: It looks like 2018
blocks.text: The design was modern then. The person who built it has moved on and the plugins have not been updated since.

blocks.title: The business changed
blocks.text: You dropped a service, added two, moved cities, and the homepage still describes the company you ran three years ago.

blocks.title: You hide the link
blocks.text: The most common reason we hear is simpler: the owner is embarrassed to send it.

blocks.title: Traffic without calls
blocks.text: Search Console shows visits and the phone stays quiet. The site is being found and failing to convince.

sections.heading: What a website redesign changes

blocks.title: Everything the visitor sees
blocks.text: New copy that says what you do now. A layout built around one clear next step. Pages that load fast on a phone, because most of your visitors are on one. A page for every service you sell, so each one can rank on its own. Forms that go to your inbox or your [CRM](/services/crm) instead of a dead mailbox.

blocks.title: Most of what Google reads
blocks.text: The structure underneath: clean titles, one heading hierarchy, schema markup, and plain question and answer sections that AI assistants can quote.

blocks.title: What stays
blocks.text: The URLs that rank, the sentences that rank, and the reviews and photos that are genuinely yours. A redesign replaces what fails and keeps what works, which is why the audit comes before the design.

sections.heading: What we check before we quote

blocks.text: Most website redesign services start with a mood board. We start with Search Console. Before the proposal we run the current site through it and pull three lists. Every URL that has earned impressions in the last 16 months. Every URL with links from other sites pointing at it. Every page that is broken, duplicated, or thin. Then the mechanical checks: mobile rendering, load speed on a throttled connection, missing titles, headings that skip levels, forms that go nowhere. The third source is analytics: which pages get visited, where visitors leave, and which forms ever get filled in. A contact page nobody reaches is a navigation problem, not a copy problem, and the audit tells the two apart.

Those lists decide the shape of the project. A site with forty pages and six that matter is a different job from a site with forty pages that all rank for something. You see the lists on the call, so the quote makes sense to you.

sections.heading: What a redesign must not break

blocks.text: This is the part most redesigns get wrong, and it is why "we redesigned the site and traffic fell off a cliff" is such a common story.

An old site has history. Some of its pages rank, some have links from other sites, and some get impressions you never noticed. A redesign that changes every URL throws that history away. Google treats the new site as a stranger.

So the URLs that earn attention either stay exactly the same or get a single hop redirect to their replacement. No chains, no 404s on pages that rank, no changed headings on a page sitting at position two. Google publishes its own rules for [site moves with URL changes](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/site-move-with-url-changes), and we follow them.
If a page already ranks in the top three, we leave its content alone and redesign around it. You cannot beat first place by editing first place.

sections.heading: Copy before layout

blocks.text: The words are usually why the old site failed, so they get rewritten first, from a call with you and from the questions your customers ask before they buy. What you do, for whom, where, and what happens next, on the first screen. Every service on its own page with a plain answer at the top. Only then does the design start, because the layout has to carry the message and not the other way round.
If your old copy has sentences that rank, they survive the rewrite. The audit tells us which ones.

sections.heading: Redesign or repair

blocks.text: Not every old site needs a rebuild. Sometimes the structure is fine and the copy is the problem. Sometimes the site is fine and the Google Business Profile is what needs work. We look at what you have before quoting, and if a cleanup is all it needs, that is what we will recommend. If it needs more than that, we will show you exactly why, with the numbers from your own Search Console.

faqs.q: Will I lose my Google rankings?
faqs.a: Not if the migration is done properly. We keep the URLs that rank, redirect the ones that must change with a single 301 each, keep the headings on pages that already rank well, and check Search Console the day we launch. blocks.text: Some owners come to us with no website at all. A Facebook page, a Google listing, maybe a logo a cousin made. Customers find them anyway, then go quiet because there is nowhere to check what the business actually does.

sections.heading: What a website has to do

blocks.text: A website is your business's digital business card. If it does not communicate what your business does, in one screen, to a stranger, it will not work no matter how good it looks.

blocks.title: Communicate
blocks.text: What you do, who you do it for, where, and what happens next. That is the first job.

blocks.title: Design it
blocks.text: Communicating is one thing and designing that communication is another. That is the second.

blocks.title: Be readable by machines
blocks.text: Google, and now the AI assistants people ask for recommendations. That is the third.
Most small business websites fail the first job. They open with a slogan, bury the phone number, and never say the city.

sections.heading: What small business website design includes

blocks.title: Copy first
blocks.text: We write it from a call with you, because the words decide the layout, not the other way round. What makes a website yours is you: the story, the branding, the personality. A template cannot supply that.

blocks.title: Design, then a hand coded build
blocks.text: We hand code every site on a modern stack instead of a drag and drop builder, which is why our pages pass Google's [Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) on a phone and why you get full control of structure and speed later.

blocks.title: Search structure built in
blocks.text: Every site ships with one page per service, one keyword per page, proper titles and headings, schema markup, and plain question and answer sections that AI assistants can lift. For a local business, that last part is what gets you named when a customer asks ChatGPT instead of Google; we wrote up the details in [AEO for local businesses](/blog/aeo-for-local-businesses). Forms connect to your inbox or your [CRM](/services/crm) so a lead never sits unread. We hand over the domain, the code, and the CMS access, and we train you on the CMS before we leave.

sections.heading: Built for the purpose, not the template

blocks.text: A service business needs a page for each service, because that is how people search and how Google ranks. A one offer business needs a landing page that does one thing well. A studio needs a portfolio that loads 40 images without stalling. A clinic needs booking.
We ask what the site is for before we open a design tool. Sometimes the answer is a three page site and a strong Google Business Profile, and we will say so.

sections.heading: Websites that get found

blocks.text: Design gets you the visitor. Structure gets you the visitor in the first place.

faqs.q: How much does small business website design cost?

faqs.q: How long does it take to build a website?
faqs.a: Four to six weeks from kickoff to launch for most projects. A focused single page site can ship faster. A larger site with custom functionality can take up to eight weeks. The timeline is in the proposal before we start.

faqs.q: Do I own my website?
faqs.a: Yes. Domain, code, content, and CMS access are all yours the day the project closes. There is no vendor lock in and no monthly fee to keep what you paid for.

faqs.q: Can I just build it myself with Wix or an AI builder?
